To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
larger individuals were more reactive than smaller individuals, but that smaller individuals were more likely than larger individuals to escape into water.

1) larger frogs showed greater escape responsiveness (longer FID and greater escape distances) than small frogs, contrary to the theoretical predictions, 2) small frogs tended to remain close to water and escaped by jumping into water, while large individuals were more likely than small individuals to jump into terrestrial cover, and 3) frogs in the open remained immobile and enhanced their crypsis, while frogs in cover showed greater responsiveness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behavioural ecology and conservation of amphibians.
the effects of body size, microhabitat selection, and density on the behaviour of frogs.
the effects of size, density and microhabitant selection on escape behaviour.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the escape behaviour of L. sphenocephalus depends on the body size of the individual and the type of microhabitat it occupies.
frogs living in open areas are less reactive than frogs living in cover, but that larger individuals in cover are more reactive than smaller individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
larger frogs are more reactive and more likely to call when fleeing.
the escape strategy of southern leopard frogs is influenced by their body size, microhabitat selection and their initial location in relation to water.
larger frogs in the open tend to flee and call, whereas smaller frogs in cover tend to remain immobile.
The main takeaway from our work is that
escape behaviour is not a simple dichotomy of fleeing or freezing, but rather a continuum of responses, which are likely to vary according to the environment that an individual is living in.
the choice to move away from a threat is not a simple decision.
escape calling in frogs is a common behaviour, and may be a way to reduce predation risk in some situations.
